stories.headline: Federal Appeals Court Rules Thousands of Social Media Addiction Lawsuits Against Meta, TikTok Can Proceed
stories.summary:
The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that thousands of lawsuits alleging Meta, TikTok, and other social media companies created addictive products harmful to young people may proceed, rejecting the platforms' attempt to have the cases dismissed at an early stage. The court determined that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act — the liability shield the companies had invoked — did not protect them from these claims at this juncture, finding the appeal was filed prematurely.

The ruling is a significant legal setback for some of the world's most valuable technology companies, which have spent years fighting to extinguish the litigation. The lawsuits, brought by thousands of families and individuals, allege the platforms deliberately engineered features to maximize engagement and foster addiction among minors, causing serious psychological harm.

The decision paves the way for the cases to advance toward discovery and potentially trial, where plaintiffs will seek to compel the companies to turn over internal research and communications about the effects of their products on young users. Meta is also separately heading into trial this week on related child safety claims.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll cited in coverage found 61 percent of Americans support stronger government oversight of social media companies, reflecting broad public concern about the issue. The ruling increases pressure on Congress and regulators to consider additional legislative action, and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have introduced bills targeting social media's effects on minors in recent sessions.

stories.headline: Rep. Lauren Boebert's Son Tyler Arrested on Felony Child Sexual Exploitation Charges
stories.summary:
Tyler Boebert, 21-year-old son of Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), was arrested Sunday by the Garfield County Sheriff's Office in Colorado on felony charges including sexual exploitation of a child, child exploitation with intent to distribute sexually exploitative material, and contributing to the delinquency of a minor. He was released after posting a $10,000 bond and has a court appearance scheduled for August 19.

According to the Denver Post, Tyler could face as many as five felonies. The charges stem from an alleged incident in early 2024, when he would have been 18 years old. The arrest followed a Garfield County Sheriff's Office investigation and a felony review by the 9th Judicial District Attorney's Office.

Rep. Boebert issued a statement saying, "I love my son. We take these allegations very seriously and pray for everyone affected during this challenging time." Tyler Boebert has a substantial prior criminal record, including 22 charges filed in 2024 — five of them felonies — related to alleged thefts, as well as two prior child abuse charges related to his young son.

The arrest draws renewed scrutiny to Boebert, a high-profile conservative congresswoman, at a time when the Republican Party is already navigating separate domestic abuse controversies surrounding other House members. Tyler Boebert has pleaded not guilty to the current charges.

stories.headline: Update: Cook Political Report Shifts Rep. Max Miller's Ohio Seat to Toss-Up Amid Domestic Violence Allegations
stories.summary:
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved Rep. Max Miller's (R-Ohio) 7th Congressional District from "Likely Republican" to "Toss-Up" on Monday, reflecting escalating political fallout from domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno — the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). The reclassification marks a dramatic shift in one of Ohio's reliably red districts.

Moreno has accused Tyler of hurling hot water at her, among other alleged acts of violence, all of which Miller has denied. Growing numbers of House Republicans have publicly called on Miller to withdraw from the race, but the withdrawal deadline has now passed, meaning Miller will remain on the November ballot regardless of further pressure.

The episode compounds Republican vulnerabilities in the House ahead of the midterms, coming alongside a separate controversy in North Carolina's 11th District, where Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure over sexual harassment allegations. State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom was selected Monday by North Carolina Republicans to replace him on the ballot with roughly 85 days until Election Day.

Democrats see both seats as pickup opportunities as the party seeks to reclaim the House majority. Republicans argue the allegations against Miller remain unproven and that their overall electoral map remains favorable, but the accumulation of candidate-quality concerns is drawing attention from national party strategists on both sides.

stories.headline: Update: Todd Blanche Sworn In as Attorney General; Trump Says He Has Not Directed Prosecution of Fauci
stories.summary:
Todd Blanche was officially sworn in as U.S. Attorney General on Monday in a ceremony at the White House, days after the Senate confirmed him in a narrow vote. Blanche, Trump's former personal attorney, becomes the second Senate-confirmed attorney general of Trump's second term, succeeding Pam Bondi, and now leads the Justice Department after months in an acting capacity.

In an Oval Office interview Monday, President Trump said he has not spoken to Blanche or Jeanine Pirro — the U.S. Attorney for Washington, D.C. — about prosecuting former NIAID Director Dr. Anthony Fauci. "I have not spoken to them about that, no," Trump told Semafor reporter Shelby Talcott. The statement came days after Senate Republicans on the Homeland Security Committee advanced recommendations related to Fauci's conduct during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Blanche's confirmation was deeply contested, with critics arguing that installing a president's personal defense attorney as the nation's top law enforcement officer poses a fundamental conflict of interest and raises concerns about the independence of the Justice Department. Supporters contend Blanche is qualified and that the confirmation process validated his fitness for the role.

The new attorney general now faces the immediate challenge of navigating a president who has openly expressed a desire to use the Justice Department to pursue political adversaries. Civil liberties organizations and Democratic lawmakers have pledged to closely monitor DOJ decisions under Blanche's leadership.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Revokes More Than 175,000 Visas
stories.summary:
The Trump administration announced Monday that it has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals, marking one of the largest single visa-revocation announcements of the administration's tenure. The State Department said the majority of cancellations stemmed from law-enforcement encounters involving criminal activity, with additional revocations tied to alleged calls for violence against U.S. citizens and other violations of entry terms.

The announcement drew immediate attention from immigration advocates and congressional Democrats, who have questioned the breadth and due-process standards applied in mass visa actions. Supporters of the policy, including Republican lawmakers and immigration enforcement groups, argue the revocations are a lawful and necessary step to remove individuals who have violated the conditions of their admission to the United States.

The scale of the action — 175,000 revocations — significantly exceeds previous single-announcement figures and affects foreign nationals across a wide range of visa categories. Critics contend that "law-enforcement encounters" is a broad standard that could encompass minor infractions, while administration officials maintain the revocations target individuals who pose public safety concerns.

The announcement is part of the administration's broader immigration enforcement push, which has included expanded deportation operations, heightened border restrictions, and increased coordination between the State Department and immigration enforcement agencies.

stories.headline: Update: Hamas Says It Has Accepted Disarmament Plan; Netanyahu Rejects Military Withdrawal
stories.summary:
Hamas announced Monday that it has accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza under which the militant group would lay down its arms and Israeli troops would withdraw from the territory. President Trump said the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas, a development that would represent a dramatic shift in the conflict if confirmed and implemented.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, rejected the terms as presented, saying Israeli forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed. The Trump administration was reported to be largely unbothered by Netanyahu's public rejection, viewing his stance as campaign rhetoric ahead of Israel's general election rather than a firm policy position.

The announcement follows months of negotiations and comes amid continued Israeli military operations in Gaza and an expanding Israeli settlement footprint in the West Bank, where large-scale land expropriations are also being planned. The Houthis in Yemen simultaneously claimed missile and drone strikes on Saudi military positions, underscoring the region's broader instability.

Skepticism remains high among analysts and regional actors about whether any disarmament agreement can be practically implemented given deep mutual distrust, ongoing hostilities, and the complex question of who would govern Gaza after Hamas. BBC international editor Jeremy Bowen noted that "the realities of politics, war, zero trust, the deaths of thousands and the destruction of Gaza will make any agreement very complicated."

stories.headline: Trump Extends Jones Act Waiver for Third Time to Ease Fuel Prices
stories.summary:
The Trump administration issued a third consecutive 90-day waiver of the Jones Act on Monday, allowing refiners to ship fuels between U.S. ports using foreign-flagged vessels in an effort to hold down gasoline and energy prices. The Jones Act, a century-old law requiring U.S.-flagged ships for domestic maritime commerce, has been a recurring target of waiver requests during periods of elevated fuel costs.

The White House framed the extension as a cost-of-living measure, arguing that allowing foreign vessels to operate in domestic shipping lanes increases supply flexibility and exerts downward pressure on consumer fuel prices. The domestic maritime industry has pushed back against the waivers, contending they undermine American shipbuilding, U.S. maritime jobs, and national security interests that the Jones Act was originally designed to protect.

The extension marks the third such waiver in the current series, indicating that the administration sees the energy price environment as sufficiently concerning to override longstanding protectionist shipping policy. Energy analysts note that Jones Act waivers provide a marginal but meaningful increase in fuel distribution efficiency, particularly along the East Coast, which relies heavily on Gulf Coast refinery output.

Critics from the maritime and labor sectors argue that repeated waivers set a precedent that gradually erodes the Jones Act's legal and political foundation, while free-market advocates and consumer groups have praised the administration for prioritizing price relief over industry protectionism.

stories.headline: WHO Warns Congo Ebola Outbreak Began Months Before It Was Declared, Now Second-Worst Ever
stories.summary:
The World Health Organization revealed Monday that the fast-moving Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began in February — roughly three months before it was officially declared on May 15 — after early cases were misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. Confirmed cases have reached approximately 4,300, with nearly 2,000 deaths, making it the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record behind the 2014–2016 West Africa crisis.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," said WHO Africa regional director Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi at a news conference in Bunia, the epicenter of the outbreak. Officials said health workers are reaching only about 30 percent of cases, with the rest dying at home, due to insecurity, unpaved roads, shortages of protective gear, and community mistrust. The outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there is no approved vaccine or recognized treatment.

The situation is further complicated by strikes by unpaid health workers, rebel group threats, and traditional burial practices that involve touching the deceased. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned last week that new cases are doubling in some hot spots. Global risk of spread is assessed as low because Ebola is not airborne, but the scale and pace of this outbreak have alarmed international health authorities.

stories.headline: Massachusetts Becomes 10th State to Remove All Gestational Age Limits on Abortion
stories.summary:
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey signed legislation Monday removing all gestational age limits on abortion, making the state the tenth in the nation — along with Washington, D.C. — to allow abortion through all stages of pregnancy based on a physician's judgment. The law repeals a prior restriction that banned abortions after 24 weeks except in life-threatening circumstances. Healey said the decision should rest with women, families, and their doctors, not politicians.

Supporters of the law argued it was necessary to protect patients carrying fetuses with severe or fatal conditions diagnosed after the 24-week threshold, citing cases of significant pain and trauma under the old restrictions. The legislation passed through the Democratic-majority state legislature before the summer recess and had been anticipated as part of a broader post-Dobbs effort by Democratic-led states to expand abortion access.

Opponents condemned the move sharply. Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, called it "barbaric" and said it exposed the failure of a purely state-by-state approach to abortion regulation, arguing the United States now stands among only eight countries worldwide permitting abortion at any point in pregnancy. The signing reignited debate over whether Congress should establish a national minimum standard — a position backed by some anti-abortion advocates and opposed by abortion rights supporters who argue federal intervention would restrict access in states like Massachusetts.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Issues Sweeping Demands as Hormuz Deal Remains Unresolved
stories.summary:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council issued a detailed list of conditions Saturday for opening the Strait of Hormuz, demanding the United States lift its maritime blockade and economic sanctions, withdraw military forces from the region, release frozen Iranian assets, pay war reparations, and cease operations against Iranian-backed groups including Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis. No formal Iran-Oman deal has been announced, but one leaked version reportedly would bar U.S. and Israeli ships from transiting the strait — a provision Washington has signaled is a non-starter. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps separately attacked a UAE vessel transiting the strait on Saturday, underscoring Tehran's leverage claims.

Critics of the administration's diplomatic approach argue Iran lacks a unified government capable of honoring any agreement, given that U.S.-Israeli strikes devastated the regime's senior leadership and left competing power centers — including the Revolutionary Guards and the Foreign Ministry — vying for control. Reports of proposed "environmental charges" of 5 to 7 percent of cargo valuations have added to uncertainty among commercial shippers about whether the strait will functionally reopen even if a deal is signed.

The Trump administration has insisted it will not pay tolls for strait passage and has not publicly accepted Iran's terms. Analysts and critics across the political spectrum warn that major concessions — particularly lifting sanctions or ending counterterrorism operations — would represent a significant strategic reversal. The standoff has kept global energy markets on edge, with the Jones Act waiver allowing foreign vessels to operate in domestic U.S. waters set to expire August 16.

stories.headline: Taylor Farms Recalls Salsa and Guacamole Sold at Walmart, Target and Trader Joe's Over Salmonella Risk
stories.summary:
Taylor Farms is recalling prepared salsa and guacamole products after federal health officials linked them to a multistate salmonella outbreak traced to fresh jalapeños supplied by Coast produce. The FDA, CDC, and local health departments announced the investigation Sunday, with recalled products distributed to 26 states through major national retailers including Walmart, Target, and Trader Joe's.

Salmonella infections can cause diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps, and can be severe or fatal in young children, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems. Consumers who purchased the affected products are advised to discard them immediately and not consume them.

The recall underscores recurring food safety vulnerabilities in fresh produce supply chains, where contamination at a single supplier can affect products sold across dozens of states under multiple brand labels. Federal investigators have not yet disclosed the number of confirmed illnesses or hospitalizations associated with this outbreak.

stories.headline: Over 60 Democrats Accuse Trump Administration of Using Military Bases as 'Traps' to Deport Noncitizen Service Members
stories.summary:
A coalition of more than 60 Democratic lawmakers sent a letter Sunday to Trump administration officials alleging that U.S. military installations are being used effectively as 'traps' to identify and deport noncitizen service members and their families. The effort is led by Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), who cited specific incidents in which individuals serving in the U.S. armed forces were targeted for removal proceedings.

The lawmakers are calling on administration officials to clarify policies governing the immigration enforcement activities that occur on or near military property, arguing that such actions undermine recruitment and retention of noncitizen service members who were promised a path to citizenship in exchange for military service. The Pentagon declined to comment publicly, stating it would reply directly to the letter's authors.

Supporters of tighter immigration enforcement argue that immigration law applies equally regardless of military affiliation and that the administration is obligated to enforce existing statutes. Critics contend that deporting individuals actively serving in the U.S. military is both legally questionable and a serious breach of faith with those who put their lives at risk for the country. The dispute reflects broader tensions over the administration's expansive immigration enforcement posture.

stories.headline: Sanders Calls on OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta CEOs to Pause AI Development, Warns of Congressional Action
stories.summary:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) sent an open letter Monday to the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta — Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Mark Zuckerberg, respectively — urging them to immediately pause artificial intelligence development. Sanders framed the request as a matter of human survival, warning that if the companies refuse, Congress will be compelled to act legislatively.

Sanders argued that the tech leaders have themselves acknowledged AI's potential for catastrophic harm, and that their failure to act on their own stated concerns is irresponsible. The letter is the senator's most aggressive public intervention on AI policy to date and signals that progressive lawmakers are moving toward more confrontational positions with major technology companies ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Critics of a development pause, including many within the AI industry, argue that halting U.S. research would cede ground to China and other competitors, and that the risks of AI are best managed through regulatory frameworks rather than blanket stops. Proponents of Sanders's position, including some AI safety researchers, maintain that the pace of development has outstripped society's ability to govern the technology. No formal legislation has been introduced accompanying the letter.

stories.headline: Health Officials Warn of Surge in Deadly Flesh-Eating Bacterial Infections Along Gulf Coast
stories.summary:
Health officials in Louisiana and Florida are warning beachgoers of a surge in Vibrio vulnificus infections this summer, a flesh-eating bacteria found in warm coastal and brackish waters. Louisiana has confirmed nine cases and five deaths so far this year, compared with an average of seven cases and one death over the same period during the prior decade. Florida has reported 14 cases and two deaths.

Vibrio vulnificus enters the body through open wounds, unhealed cuts, tattoos, or piercings that come into contact with seawater, and also through consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish such as oysters. The fatality rate for the most severe infections can reach one in five. Officials urge anyone whose wound becomes red, swollen, or painful after water exposure to seek immediate medical care and inform their provider about the exposure.

Scientists say rising ocean temperatures linked to climate change are enabling the bacteria to proliferate and spread northward, with the northernmost reported cases shifting approximately 30 miles per year. Severe illness is most common in elderly patients, those with weakened immune systems, or individuals with underlying conditions such as liver disease or diabetes. The Gulf Coast summer season, combined with record ocean temperatures reported last month, has created conditions particularly favorable to bacterial growth.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Shifts to Economic Pressure on Iran, Admits No Direct Talks and Munitions Shortage
stories.summary:
President Trump has reversed course on Iran negotiations, telling Axios he is "low-keying it" and will rely on economic pressure rather than the threat of fresh military strikes to force a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump acknowledged the U.S. is only "semi-negotiating" with Tehran, walking back weeks of claims that a deal was imminent. Iran's foreign minister confirmed there are no direct talks, only indirect message exchanges through intermediaries.

The shift follows Iran's Supreme National Security Council issuing a sweeping list of demands Saturday — including full U.S. military withdrawal from the region, war damage reimbursement, and an end to the blockade and sanctions — which former Defense Secretary Mark Esper called "beyond the pale" and "ridiculous." Esper warned on ABC's This Week that Iran appears to believe it has the upper hand after more than five months of conflict.

Critics from both parties are questioning whether economic pressure alone can work. Former Israeli military intelligence official Danny Citrinowicz wrote that Iran has "spent decades operating under intense economic pressure" and has repeatedly shown it can absorb pain without abandoning core strategic interests. Reports also confirm U.S. stockpiles of premier offensive and defensive missiles are nearly exhausted after sustained strikes, limiting Trump's military options.

The Iran standoff carries enormous global economic stakes: oil prices have risen as the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of the world's oil passes, remains closed. Trump's reliance on sanctions and a port blockade rather than military action represents a significant strategic pivot, with no clear timeline for resolution.

stories.headline: South Carolina Holds Senate Primary to Replace Lindsey Graham, With Foreign Policy Legacy on the Ballot
stories.summary:
South Carolina voters head to the polls Tuesday to choose a Republican Senate nominee to fill the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died of heart problems on July 11. The leading contenders are Graham's sister Darline Graham, appointed by the governor to fill the remainder of the term and now running for the full six-year seat, and Republican House members Ralph Norman and Russell Fry. The race is expected to be competitive enough that it may go to a runoff on August 25.

Analysts note the election marks a generational and philosophical inflection point for South Carolina's Senate delegation. Graham was one of Congress's most prominent foreign policy hawks, cultivating relationships with allied foreign leaders and championing U.S. military engagement abroad for more than two decades. None of the leading candidates has signaled any intention of following that path, and observers say South Carolina voters are not demanding it.

Graham's former staffers credit his repeated reelection victories less to his foreign policy profile than to his record of delivering federal resources to the state — including military installations, infrastructure funding, and the multi-decade dredging of the Port of Charleston to accommodate larger cargo vessels. That project is widely credited with transforming South Carolina's economy.

The outcome will affect the balance of the Senate and signal whether Republican primary voters in a deep-red state continue to reward institutionalist conservatives or prefer members who keep a narrower focus on domestic issues. A runoff, if triggered, would be held August 25.

stories.headline: Connecticut Democratic Primary Tests Chris Murphy's Influence Ahead of Potential 2028 Presidential Bid
stories.summary:
Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy is putting his political capital on the line Tuesday in a Democratic House primary, backing 78-year-old Rep. John Larson against former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, in what has become a closely watched test of Murphy's standing ahead of widely discussed 2028 presidential ambitions. The race in Connecticut's heavily Democratic 1st Congressional District features generational politics at its center, with Bronin arguing the district needs younger, more energetic leadership to counter the Trump administration.

Larson, who has served in the House since 1999 and is running for a 14th term, drew scrutiny last February when he froze on the House floor due to a complex partial seizure linked to a pre-existing heart condition. His campaign has leaned on his progressive voting record, including his push to impeach Trump, as well as Murphy's high-profile endorsement. Murphy told the Washington Examiner he backs Larson because of his effectiveness on gun violence funding and defense industry jobs.

Bronin's campaign has received financial backing from technology and AI sector donors, a contrast his opponents have highlighted. Murphy's team dismissed that support, with Larson's campaign manager calling Murphy's endorsement worth more than "all the AI data center billionaires behind Bronin combined." The race is also a four-way contest, increasing the odds that no candidate clears a decisive majority.

For Murphy, a Larson loss could complicate his national profile at a moment when Democratic primary voters have shown increasing willingness to replace veteran incumbents with younger challengers. Political strategists say a Larson victory would validate Murphy's endorsement and reinforce his status as a credible kingmaker within the party.

stories.headline: World's Oceans Hit Record-High Temperatures for July as El Niño Develops
stories.summary:
The world's oceans reached their hottest recorded temperatures for any July in history last month, according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service. The average sea surface temperature outside polar regions hit 20.96 degrees Celsius, surpassing the previous July record of 20.89 degrees Celsius set in 2023. July 2026 was also the joint second-warmest July on record globally, with temperatures 1.47 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial averages.

Scientists attribute the spike in part to developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, a natural warming pattern that, combined with human-driven climate change, amplifies temperature extremes. Sea surface temperatures set records along Europe's Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread marine heatwaves. Western Europe recorded its hottest combined June and July on record, averaging 2.79 degrees Celsius above normal.

The consequences of ocean warming extend well beyond water temperatures. Warmer seas drive sea level rise through thermal expansion, intensify tropical storms and their rainfall, and have contributed to mass coral bleaching events worldwide. Scientists at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts noted that dry soils across Western Europe — parched by an exceptional run of heat waves — have reduced the land's natural cooling capacity, further amplifying surface temperatures.

The data arrives as Western Europe contends with its fifth heat wave of the season and the United Kingdom braces for a potential official drought declaration. Copernicus researchers said the findings are consistent with projections that climate change is making extreme heat events both more frequent and more severe.

stories.headline: At Least 13 Killed as Ukraine Strikes Oil Refinery Deep Inside Russia's Tatarstan Region
stories.summary:
A Ukrainian drone strike on the city of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan republic killed at least 13 people — including one child — and injured 75 more, Russian officials said Monday. The attack, which lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, is among the deadliest single Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. Tatarstan's regional head declared a period of mourning.

Ukraine's Armed Forces confirmed that the Tanevo oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk was struck, and Ukrainian defense technology manufacturer FirePoint said its FP-1 drones were used in the attack. The city sits more than 1,100 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, underscoring Kyiv's expanding long-range strike capabilities. Russia's Investigative Committee said civilians uninvolved in military operations were among the victims; the BBC has not independently verified this claim.

Kyiv has not officially commented on the strike but has recently escalated attacks on Russian energy and logistics infrastructure it says funds Moscow's war effort. Russia simultaneously claimed its air defenses shot down more than 450 Ukrainian drones overnight. In a parallel development, five people were killed in a Russian artillery strike on Kharkiv, and Russian missiles also struck near Kyiv last week, killing 21.

The strike represents a significant escalation in the pattern of deep strikes inside Russia, raising questions about both the trajectory of the conflict and the vulnerability of Russian industrial infrastructure far from the front lines. Moscow condemned the attack on what it characterized as civilian areas, while Ukraine frames such strikes as legitimate targeting of war-sustaining economic assets.

stories.headline: Update: Typhoon Dolphin Forces Evacuation of Over One Million in Eastern China, Triggers Massive Disruptions
stories.summary:
Chinese authorities evacuated more than one million people from homes across eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall Sunday in Zhejiang province with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (94 mph). Authorities issued their highest-level red alert for the storm, the strongest to hit China this year. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone, and major tourist attractions including parts of Disneyland and Legoland were closed.

Dolphin made two landfalls — first in Yuhuan and then in Wenzhou — before being downgraded to a tropical storm. Despite the downgrade, authorities warned of torrential rains, severe flooding, and landslide risks through Wednesday as the storm tracks north. Provinces including Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang face heavy rain forecasts, with some areas expected to receive 250–500mm over several days.

Wenzhou authorities relocated approximately 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Taizhou, some 390,000 people were evacuated. A nine-year-old boy from Wenling is missing after reportedly being swept into the sea; Chinese officials have not announced confirmed casualties. Maritime authorities suspended passenger ferry routes and halted offshore construction projects along the Fujian coast.

The storm traveled an unusually long distance of 6,000 kilometers before landfall, giving it a lifespan more than three times that of an average typhoon and an exceptionally large circulation. Chinese state media reported that two people were detained for spreading AI-generated misinformation about the storm's damage on social media.

stories.headline: Wildfires Near Spokane Force 60,000 to Evacuate, Destroy at Least 600 Structures
stories.summary:
Fast-moving wildfires in and around Spokane, Washington — the state's second-largest city — forced the evacuation of approximately 60,000 people over the weekend and destroyed at least 600 homes, businesses, and other structures, authorities said Sunday. The fires burned roughly 8.2 square miles in the Spokane area and remained uncontained, with officials warning that dry weather in the coming days would sustain dangerous conditions. Evacuees included patients from a Veterans Affairs hospital in the city.

Across Washington state, approximately 390 square miles have burned, and dozens of additional wildfires stretched the capacity of federal, state, and local firefighting agencies. A separate fire that has burned nearly 525 square miles of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon — threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures — entered its tenth day. No fatalities or missing persons had been confirmed as of Sunday, though officials cautioned it was early in the response.

Washington Governor Jay Inslee said he spoke with President Trump about the wildfires. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, appearing at a news conference in Spokane with federal and state officials, warned that the region is not out of danger. Investigators had not yet determined the cause of the blazes.

The scale of the Spokane fires — in an urban and suburban setting — marks a significant escalation in the ongoing Western wildfire season. Aerial footage showed neighborhoods reduced to foundations with only chimneys remaining standing, drawing comparisons to previous urban wildfire disasters.

stories.headline: Western Europe Sets New Temperature Record as Continent Faces Fifth Heat Wave of Season
stories.summary:
France is bracing for its fifth heat wave alert of the summer season, with national weather agency Météo-France warning of temperatures approaching 40°C (104°F) in southeastern France beginning Tuesday. Across Western Europe, a prolonged stretch of extreme heat that began in May has contributed to major wildfires, record-breaking droughts, new national temperature records, and thousands of projected heat-related deaths. The average temperature for Western Europe's June-July period reached 21.62°C (70.92°F), breaking the previous record set in 2022, according to the European climate agency Copernicus.

July also saw the highest average sea surface temperature ever recorded for the month across ice-free oceans globally — 20.96°C (69.73°F) — surpassing the 2023 record. Scientists attribute the extreme conditions to a combination of accelerating human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño weather pattern. Globally, 2026 is currently the third-hottest year on record behind 2024 and 2025, but scientists say there is an increasing chance it could become the hottest year ever recorded by December.

The Rhine and Danube rivers have both receded to historically low levels, with photos showing people walking on sandbars normally submerged beneath the rivers in Germany and Hungary. Climatologists warn that as soils dry out under prolonged heat, they lose their natural cooling capacity, creating a feedback loop that allows temperatures to build more readily.

The European heat emergency reflects a broader global trend, with scientists noting that extreme heat events that once occurred once per decade are now recurring multiple times per season across the continent. Public health authorities have urged residents — particularly the elderly — to stay indoors, as projections of excess mortality from the season continue to rise.
